item.qtcraft.armor_stand.description: Place it on a block and dress it: right click with armour or an item puts it on, with an empty hand you take it back. Two quick hits (the second after your attack cooldown, within a second) break it; it drops itself and everything it wears. The command /armorstand poses it.
item.qtcraft.minecart.description: Set it down on a rail and get in with a use; sneak to get out. It rolls on along the track, faster downhill; the forward key pushes it while you ride. One hit breaks it.
item.qtcraft.chest_minecart.description: A minecart that carries a chest of {qtcraft:chest.slots} slots. Use it to look inside; it cannot be ridden. A Signal Hopper under its rail empties it, and broken it drops itself and what it carried.
item.qtcraft.hopper_minecart.description: A minecart that carries a Signal Hopper: it pulls items from a container above its rail and picks up items lying on its way, one item per hopper step. A powered activator rail stops it pulling until it passes an unpowered one. A Signal Hopper under its rail empties it.
handbook.slot.head: Head
handbook.table.armourText: Armour is worn in four slots next to the character in the inventory: drag it there, shift-click it or right-click with it in the hand. Every armour point takes 4 % off the blows of creatures and the burns of lava and magma, up to 20 points (80 %); falls and hunger go through. Each such hit wears every worn piece by a quarter of the damage (at least 1); a piece breaks when its durability is used up. Two worn pieces of the same kind in the crafting grid make one with both durabilities plus 5 %.
mob.qtcraft.caped_mannequin.description: A mannequin wearing the green cape. It walks about slowly, so the cape swings; it never appears by itself, the showcase world has one at the character stand.
chapter.qtcraft.creative.modes.title: Survival and creative
chapter.qtcraft.creative.modes.text: Every player has a game mode. In **survival** you gather, craft, eat and can die. In **creative** you build freely: every block and item without limit, flying, blocks break at the first strike, nothing hurts you and you never get hungry. A new world asks for the mode of its players in the main menu (**Game mode**); operators change it with `/gamemode creative` or `/gamemode survival` (also for another player: `/gamemode creative Alice`), and `/defaultgamemode` sets the mode of players who join for the first time.
chapter.qtcraft.creative.flying.title: Flying
chapter.qtcraft.creative.flying.text: Tap **{key.jump}** twice quickly to take off or to stop flying. While flying, **{key.jump}** rises, **{key.sneak}** sinks and **{key1.sprint}** doubles the speed ({player.flySpeed} m/s, sprinting {player.flySprintSpeed} m/s); the view widens a little. Sinking onto the ground lands you and ends the flight. The showcase world has a platform high above the ground that only flyers reach.
chapter.qtcraft.creative.inventory.title: Creative inventory
chapter.qtcraft.creative.inventory.text: **{key.inventory}** opens the creative inventory: every block and item of the game and of the loaded mods, sorted into tabs (blocks, building parts, tools and armour, food, other items) with a search that finds names in your language, English names and ids like `oak_planks`. A left click takes a full stack, a right click one item, a shift-click puts a full stack straight into the inventory; click a slot to put it there. The bin deletes a stack. **Crafting and armour** leads to the usual inventory with the crafting grid and the armour slots.
chapter.qtcraft.creative.rules.title: Rules in creative mode
chapter.qtcraft.creative.rules.text:
- Blocks break at once (even bedrock) and drop nothing; chests and furnaces still lose their contents.
- Placing a block keeps your stack, a poured bucket stays full.
- No damage except `/kill`; creatures leave you alone; food stays as it is.
- **Middle mouse** or **{key1.pickBlock}** puts the block you look at into your hand; in survival this selects it when it is in your inventory.
chapter.qtcraft.creative.switching.title: Changing between the modes
chapter.qtcraft.creative.switching.text: Survival and creative each have their own inventory and armour. Changing the mode puts the current ones aside and brings back those of the other mode, so creative items never end up in your survival inventory. Health and food stay as they were. Chests belong to the world: what you put into a chest in creative mode is there in survival too.
block.qtcraft.farmland.description: Tilled earth for crops. Water within four blocks keeps it wet, and crops grow twice as fast on wet farmland. Rain falling on it wets it too. Without water, rain and crops it dries out and turns back into dirt.
block.qtcraft.dirt_path.description: A trodden path, a little lower than the ground beside it. Villages lay their side roads with it; a shovel used on the top of grass or dirt makes one (each path wears the shovel a little, not in creative mode). It drops dirt, a hoe turns it into farmland, and a solid block placed on it presses it back into dirt.
block.qtcraft.wheat_crop.description: Grows from wheat seeds on farmland in eight stages. Ripe wheat gives wheat and seeds; unripe plants only give a seed back.
block.qtcraft.carrot_crop.description: Grows from a carrot on farmland in four stages. Ripe plants give two to four carrots.
block.qtcraft.potato_crop.description: Grows from a potato on farmland in four stages. Ripe plants give two to four potatoes.
block.qtcraft.pumpkin_stem.description: Grows from pumpkin seeds on farmland. When ripe it puts a pumpkin on a free neighbouring block of farmland, dirt or grass, one at a time.
block.qtcraft.melon_stem.description: Grows from melon seeds on farmland. When ripe it puts a melon on a free neighbouring block of farmland, dirt or grass, one at a time.
block.qtcraft.pumpkin.description: Grows next to a pumpkin stem and wild in plains and taiga. Gives pumpkin seeds and pumpkin pie.
block.qtcraft.melon.description: Grows next to a melon stem and wild in forests and swamps. Breaks into three to seven slices.
block.qtcraft.wild_carrots.description: Wild carrots do not grow in the base world: carrots come from the fields of villages. Mods (and later oases) can place them with the feature of the same name.
block.qtcraft.wild_potatoes.description: Wild potatoes do not grow in the base world: potatoes come from the fields of villages. Mods (and later oases) can place them with the feature of the same name.
item.qtcraft.wooden_hoe.description: Tills grass and dirt into farmland. Each tilled block wears it a little.
item.qtcraft.stone_hoe.description: Tills grass and dirt into farmland; lasts longer than wood.
item.qtcraft.iron_hoe.description: Tills grass and dirt into farmland; lasts long.
item.qtcraft.golden_hoe.description: Tills grass and dirt into farmland, but wears out quickly.
item.qtcraft.diamond_hoe.description: Tills grass and dirt into farmland and lasts very long.
item.qtcraft.wheat_seeds.description: Found in tall grass. Planted on farmland they grow into wheat; dropped onto free farmland they plant themselves.
item.qtcraft.wheat.description: Harvested from ripe wheat. Three make a bread; animals like sheep love it.
item.qtcraft.bread.description: Baked from three wheat; a good meal.
item.qtcraft.carrot.description: A snack and the seed of carrot plants. Pigs follow their love for it.
item.qtcraft.potato.description: Barely filling raw; plant it on farmland or bake it in a furnace.
item.qtcraft.baked_potato.description: A potato baked in a furnace; as filling as bread.
item.qtcraft.pumpkin_seeds.description: Four from a pumpkin. Planted on farmland they grow into a pumpkin stem.
item.qtcraft.melon_seeds.description: One from a melon slice. Planted on farmland they grow into a melon stem.
item.qtcraft.melon_slice.description: A juicy bite; nine make a whole melon again.
item.qtcraft.pumpkin_pie.description: Pumpkin, sugar and wheat baked into the most filling food of the farm.
item.qtcraft.sugar.description: Made from sugar cane; sweetens a pumpkin pie.
item.qtcraft.raw_mutton.description: Meat of a sheep; better cooked in a furnace.
item.qtcraft.cooked_mutton.description: Mutton cooked in a furnace; good food.
handbook.unit.crop: %1 stages, ripe after about %2 min on wet farmland, %3 min on dry
handbook.unit.fruit: about every %1 min, one at a time
handbook.fact.plantsItself: Dropped seed plants itself on farmland
handbook.unit.breeding: again after %1 min, young grow up in %2 min
chapter.qtcraft.farming.soil.title: Farmland
chapter.qtcraft.farming.soil.text: Use a hoe on grass or dirt with air above it to make farmland; every tilled block wears the hoe once (not in creative mode). Water within four blocks around it, at the same height or one above, keeps farmland wet. Without water it dries out; dry farmland without a crop on it turns back into dirt, and so does farmland under a full block. Walking and jumping on farmland do not trample it.
chapter.qtcraft.farming.crops.title: Crops
chapter.qtcraft.farming.crops.text: Plant wheat seeds, carrots or potatoes on farmland. Crops grow in stages on random ticks (each block gets one about every {farming.randomTickSeconds} s) while their chunk is loaded; time while the world is closed does not count. They grow twice as fast on wet farmland and need light of at least 9, from the sky or from lamps. Break a ripe crop for the harvest; an unripe one only gives back what was planted. Seeds come from tall grass. Growing wheat, carrots and potatoes are found only in the fields of villages: harvest a ripe plant there for your first carrots and potatoes (a zombie now and then drops one too).
chapter.qtcraft.farming.stems.title: Pumpkins and melons
chapter.qtcraft.farming.stems.text: Pumpkin and melon seeds grow into stems. A ripe stem puts its fruit onto a free neighbouring block of farmland, dirt or grass, one at a time; harvest the fruit and the stem grows another. Leave a free side next to every stem. A pumpkin gives four seeds, a melon slice one; pumpkins and melons also grow wild.
chapter.qtcraft.farming.seeds.title: Seeds plant themselves
chapter.qtcraft.farming.seeds.text: Seeds, carrots and potatoes lying on free farmland plant one of their stack by themselves (checked every {farming.seedCheckSeconds} s, with a high chance). A stack whose own block is taken, or that holds more, plants into the free farmland right around it, one seed per check, so drops that merged into one stack still plant the whole patch. Flowing water carries dropped items along its current; still water does not. A field washed off with water from behind replants itself where the drops come to rest; collect the rest of the harvest.
chapter.qtcraft.farming.animals.title: Breeding animals
chapter.qtcraft.farming.animals.text: Feed pigs with carrots or potatoes and sheep with wheat: a fed adult falls in love for a while and walks towards another one of its kind in love; two that see each other get a young one. Parents rest five minutes before they breed again; a young one grows up in twenty minutes, each feeding takes {farming.youngFeedShare} % of that time off. Young animals leave nothing behind. Crowded places get no more young ones.
chapter.qtcraft.farming.food.title: Food from the farm
chapter.qtcraft.farming.food.text: Bread from three wheat, baked potatoes from the furnace, pumpkin pie from a pumpkin, sugar and wheat, melon slices and carrots to eat on the way. Carrots and potatoes are planted when used on farmland and eaten elsewhere.
chapter.qtcraft.texture_packs.choosing.t: **Settings → Texture packs** changes how blocks, items, creatures, your character and the icons look. **QtCraft HD** paints the game's own textures at 32, 64 or 128 pixels with finer detail; **Storybook** is a small pack of drawn images with outlines and warm colours. Changes apply at once, also in a running world, and only on your computer: other players keep their own choice.
chapter.qtcraft.texture_packs.order.text: Switch on up to 16 packs. A pack you switch on goes to the top; the arrows change the order. For every texture the highest pack that has it wins, then the next one, and finally the game's own texture, so a small pack can change just a few blocks.
chapter.qtcraft.texture_packs.own.title: Your own packs
chapter.qtcraft.texture_packs.own.text: A pack is a folder with a **texturepack.json** and PNG images (or texture descriptions) in **textures/qtcraft/**, one per texture, all of the same size from 16 to 512 pixels. **Open texture pack folder** in the settings shows where they go; **Reload** reads them again after a change. Mods can bring packs of their own.
chapter.qtcraft.texture_packs.problems.t: A damaged image or one of the wrong size is skipped and listed under its pack; that texture then comes from the next pack. Very large packs are shown at a lower resolution when the graphics card or the memory would not take them, and the settings say so.
block.qtcraft.signal_dust.description: The wire of every circuit. It carries a signal of strength 15 from a source and loses one per block, connects to its neighbours, climbs up and down blocks and powers the block it lies on and the blocks its lines point at.
block.qtcraft.signal_torch.description: A source that is on unless the block it stands on or hangs at is powered: the inverter of Signal Dust. It powers the block above it strongly. Switched too fast it burns out for a while.
block.qtcraft.signal_torch_off.descripti: A Signal Torch whose block is powered, or one that burnt out.
block.qtcraft.lever.description: Switches a signal of strength 15 on and off. It powers its neighbours and the block it hangs on.
block.qtcraft.stone_button.description: Gives a short signal of one second when pressed.
block.qtcraft.oak_button.description: Gives a signal of one and a half seconds when pressed.
block.qtcraft.stone_pressure_plate.descr: Gives a signal while a player or a creature stands on it.
block.qtcraft.oak_pressure_plate.descrip: Gives a signal while anything lies or stands on it, items and armour stands too.
block.qtcraft.signal_repeater.descriptio: Passes a signal from back to front at full strength after a delay of one to four steps (use it to change the delay). A powered repeater pointing at its side locks it.
block.qtcraft.signal_lamp.description: Lights up at once while it is powered and goes dark a moment after.
block.qtcraft.chunk_loader.description: Keeps its chunk loaded while no player is near, with every chunk its circuits connect to, so farms and machines go on working. Each player may place a few (chunkLoadersPerPlayer, 4 by default); only so many work in a world (chunkLoaders, 64).
block.qtcraft.signal_piston.description: Pushes up to twelve blocks in front of it while powered, chests and furnaces with their contents, and pushes players and creatures along.
block.qtcraft.sticky_signal_piston.descr: A piston that pulls the block in front of it back when it retracts; a too short signal makes it let go of the block.
block.qtcraft.signal_piston_head.descrip: The head of an extended piston.
block.qtcraft.signal_ore.description: Ore deep below that gives Signal Dust; needs an iron pickaxe.
block.qtcraft.rail.description: Track for minecarts. It needs a solid block below, joins the rails beside it and climbs one block towards a rail above.
block.qtcraft.powered_rail.description: Rail that speeds carts up while it gets Signal Dust power and brakes them to a stop while it does not. Power passes along a line of powered rails for eight rails. A cart standing on it in front of a block starts away from the block. It does not bend.
block.qtcraft.detector_rail.description: Rail that gives a signal while a minecart is on it, like a pressure plate. A Signal Comparator behind it reads how full a chest or hopper cart on it is. It does not bend.
block.qtcraft.activator_rail.description: Rail that acts on carts while it gets power: the rider gets out and a hopper cart stops pulling; unpowered, it lets hopper carts pull again. Power passes along a line of them for eight rails. It does not bend.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.wire.title: The wire
chapter.qtcraft.signal.wire.text: Signal Dust comes from Signal ore deep below (an iron pickaxe or better). Laid on a block it becomes a wire: it connects to the dust next to it, climbs up the side of a block when nothing opaque lies on it, and runs down the side of a block that is not opaque. A lone dust is a dot that powers all four sides; one connection makes a straight line that points on; more make corners and crosses. A signal starts with strength 15 and loses one per block of wire, so after fifteen blocks it is gone; a Signal Repeater starts it at 15 again.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.power.title: Powered blocks
chapter.qtcraft.signal.power.text: Full solid blocks like stone carry power on. A lever or button powers the block it hangs on strongly, a plate the block below, a Signal Torch the block above, a repeater the block in front. A strongly powered block powers dust and slots around it. Dust powers the block it lies on and the blocks its lines point at only weakly: a weakly powered block still powers lamps, pistons, doors, torches and repeaters next to it, but never other dust. Glass, pistons and slabs carry nothing.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.sources.title: Sources
chapter.qtcraft.signal.sources.text: A lever stays on or off. A stone button gives a signal for one second, a wooden one for one and a half. A wooden pressure plate is pressed by anything lying or standing on it, a stone one only by players and creatures; it springs back about a second after it is free. A Signal Torch is on unless its block is powered, two ticks after the change: an inverter. Switched on and off more than eight times within three seconds it burns out for eight seconds. A Signal Repeater passes a signal from back to front after one to four steps of two ticks (use it to change the delay); a short pulse comes out as long as its delay, and a powered repeater pointing at its side locks it.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.slots.title: Slots
chapter.qtcraft.signal.slots.text: What reacts to a signal is called a slot. A Signal Lamp lights at once and goes dark a moment after it loses power. Doors, trapdoors and fence gates open when their power comes and close when it goes; in between players still open and close them by hand. Iron doors and iron trapdoors open only by signal, not by hand.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.pistons.title: Pistons
chapter.qtcraft.signal.pistons.text: A powered Signal Piston pushes up to {signal.pushLimit} blocks in front of it by one. Chests, barrels and furnaces move with everything in them. Plants, torches, dust and liquids in the way break; bedrock, obsidian and extended pistons stop it. Players, creatures, items and armour stands in the way are pushed along. A Sticky Signal Piston pulls the block in front of its head back when it retracts. A piston is not powered through its front.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.hoppers.title: Hoppers
chapter.qtcraft.signal.hoppers.text: A Signal Hopper moves {signal.hopperItemsPerSecond} items a second: it passes one item from its first slot that fits into the container its spout points at, then takes one from the container above it. Without a container above it collects items lying in its bowl or on the block above it, also through a slab, a carpet, farmland or any block that does not fill its cell; under a full block it collects nothing. Into a furnace it puts items from above into the input and from the side into the fuel slot (fuel only); from below it takes the furnace's output. Any signal locks it. A hopper with nothing to do rests until something around it changes, so idle hoppers cost nothing. Several hoppers that put items into one full container at the same time: the one from above first, then the others by item, equal items all or none.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.comparators.title: Comparators
chapter.qtcraft.signal.comparators.text: A Signal Comparator passes on the strength from its back, two ticks later. A chest, barrel, hopper, dispenser or furnace behind it (also behind one full block) gives its fullness instead: nothing in it is 0, otherwise 1 plus 14 times how full its slots are on average. Ripe wheat, carrots and potatoes are read too (0 to 15 by their stage). In compare mode a stronger side input (dust, a repeater or comparator pointing at it) switches it off; in subtract mode the side input is taken off. Use it to switch the mode. A hopper sorter whose filter is read by a comparator needs an inverter to lock the hopper below the filter: a Signal Torch burns out when one kind of item comes at full hopper speed (eight times off within three seconds) and the filter then drains; a comparator in subtract mode with a lever behind it does not burn out (the showcase's sorter).
chapter.qtcraft.signal.observers.title: Observers
chapter.qtcraft.signal.observers.text: A Signal Observer watches the block in front of its face. When that block changes its state (placed, broken, a crop grows, dust changes its strength, a door opens), it sends a pulse of two ticks out of its back, two ticks later. Changes of what is inside a container do not count. Two observers looking at each other make a fast clock.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.dispensers.title: Dispensers and droppers
chapter.qtcraft.signal.dispensers.text: When their power comes, a Signal Dispenser and a Signal Dropper eject one item from a random slot four ticks later (powered like a piston, also through the block above). A dropper facing a container puts the item into it, otherwise it throws it out. A dispenser pours water and lava buckets, takes a liquid with an empty bucket, puts armour on a player or armour stand in front and throws everything else out, also in front of a container. Seeds, carrots and potatoes are thrown, never planted: they plant themselves when they land on free farmland.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.quirks.title: Known quirks
chapter.qtcraft.signal.quirks.text: Pistons are also powered by whatever would power the block above them, but only notice it when a block next to them changes: a piston can sit powered and still until then (a block update detector, BUD). The game rule quasiConnectivity switches this off for a world; a piston can refuse it in its data. A pulse shorter than a piston's two-tick extension (down to one that comes and goes within a single tick) pushes the block and lets go of it: a sticky piston leaves its block one further (block spitting). Torch clocks burn out, and repeaters keep their delays.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.rotation.title: Same in every place
chapter.qtcraft.signal.rotation.text: A circuit behaves the same at every coordinate and in every rotation. Everything that switches in the same step decides on the world as it was before the step and switches together. When two pistons want the same block or cell in the same step, both stay where they are.
chapter.qtcraft.signal.multiplayer.title: On a server
chapter.qtcraft.signal.multiplayer.text: Circuits run on the server; everyone sees the same states. Levers, buttons and repeaters switch at most {signal.switchesPerSecond} times a second per player. The work of all circuits per tick is limited; a huge machine slows down instead of stopping the server.
chapter.qtcraft.rails.track.title: Laying track
chapter.qtcraft.rails.track.text: Rails need a solid block below them. A rail joins the rails beside it on its own: one neighbour makes a straight piece that points at it, two at a right angle make a curve, a line of three or four keeps the straight line (a branch does not bend it). A rail with a rail one block higher beside it rises towards it, so a track climbs and descends one block at a time. Where the neighbours decide nothing, a new rail runs the way you look. Rails behave the same in every direction.
chapter.qtcraft.rails.carts.title: Minecarts
chapter.qtcraft.rails.carts.text: Use a minecart on a rail to set it down. A cart keeps rolling along the track, round curves and over slopes: downhill it speeds up, uphill it slows down and may roll back, and it slowly loses speed on the flat (a ridden cart much more slowly than an empty one). At the end of a track it stops in front of a block and flies on otherwise (see below). Carts that run into each other pass their speed on; walking into a cart pushes it. A cart without rails under it stops after a short slide, or coasts far on ice. One hit breaks a cart; it drops itself.
chapter.qtcraft.rails.riding.title: Riding
chapter.qtcraft.rails.riding.text: Use a cart to get in and sneak to get out; you land beside it. While you ride, the forward key pushes the cart along the way you look. The server moves the cart and its rider, so everyone sees you ride the same way.
chapter.qtcraft.rails.pistons.title: Pistons and carts
chapter.qtcraft.rails.jumps.text: A cart that reaches the end of a track with a block in front of it stops there. At an open end it keeps its speed and flies on: it falls, and off the top of a ramp it jumps. Where it lands it stops after a short slide, coasts far on ice, or, landing on a rail, rolls on along it with its speed along the track (landing across the track it stands until the next cart bumps it on). A rider flies with the cart and takes no fall damage.
chapter.qtcraft.rails.jumps.title: Track ends and jumps
chapter.qtcraft.rails.pistons.text: A Signal Piston pushes a cart in front of its head or in front of the block it moves, like any other body; a piston pushing a line of rails moves the rails and the cart on them. A rider stays in the cart.
chapter.qtcraft.rails.signal.title: Powered, detector and activator rails
chapter.qtcraft.rails.signal.text: Three rails work with Signal Dust. A powered rail speeds a cart up while it gets power, up to the top speed, and brakes it to a stop while it does not; a cart standing on a powered rail with a block at one end starts away from the block. A detector rail gives a signal while a cart is on it; a Signal Comparator behind it reads the contents of a chest or hopper cart on it. An activator rail with power puts the rider out and stops a hopper cart pulling; without power it lets hopper carts pull again. Power given to one powered or activator rail passes along the line of rails of the same kind for eight rails, also up and down slopes, and goes when the power goes. These rails do not bend: where two rails meet at a corner they keep their line. Everything works the same in every direction.
chapter.qtcraft.rails.containers.title: Chest and hopper carts
chapter.qtcraft.rails.containers.text: A chest cart carries a chest: use it to open its screen like a chest. A hopper cart carries a Signal Hopper and pulls one item at a time from a container above its rail, or picks up items lying on its rail; it rests between items like a hopper. A Signal Hopper under a rail takes the items out of a chest or hopper cart standing above it, one at a time, and passes them on; Signal Hoppers can carry rails. Broken, a cart drops itself and what it carried. Carts keep their contents when their chunk is saved or unloaded.
chapter.qtcraft.fire.burning.title: Burning
chapter.qtcraft.fire.burning.text: Fire stands on a solid block or next to a flammable one, and it lights everything around it with light 15. About every {fire.stepSecondsMin} to {fire.stepSecondsMax} seconds it takes a step and grows older; after {fire.maxAge} steps at the latest it goes out. Without a flammable block next to it, it goes out after {fire.ageWithoutFuel} steps, so fire on stone or sand burns down quickly. Fire whose ground or fuel goes away goes out at once, and water flowing in washes it away. Breaking fire puts it out.
chapter.qtcraft.fire.lighting.title: Lighting fire
chapter.qtcraft.fire.lighting.text: Flint and steel lights fire in front of the face of a block you use it on, if fire can stand there: on a solid block or next to a flammable one. Each fire wears it by one use; in creative mode it does not wear. A Signal Dispenser holding flint and steel lights the cell in front of it when it fires; if nothing can burn there, the flint and steel stays inside. Lava now and then sets fire to the air right next to it when that air touches a flammable block, but only when something next to the lava changes or it flows: a still lava lake does not set the woods around it alight. Every new fire is a spark of its own and keeps the limits below. Breaking or punching fire puts it out, also in creative mode.
chapter.qtcraft.fire.spreading.title: Spreading
chapter.qtcraft.fire.spreading.text: Each step may burn away the flammable blocks next to the fire: they turn into fire or into air, and nothing drops. It may also light the air around it next to flammable blocks, most readily above it. How readily a block catches fire and how quickly it burns away depends on the block: leaves, wool, grass and flowers burn readily, logs, planks and coal blocks slowly; stone, earth, glass and metal never burn. Fire on a magma block burns forever without spreading: a hearth. A new fire is as old as the one that lit it, so a fire front always dies out.
chapter.qtcraft.fire.limits.title: Limits
chapter.qtcraft.fire.limits.text: Fire spreads at most {fire.spreadRadius} blocks from the spark it began with, so a single spark never burns down a whole forest or village. It never spreads into chunks that are not loaded. A chunk holds at most {fire.perChunk} fires and the world {fire.total}; beyond, no new fire is lit. The game rule `fireSpread` (`/gamerule fireSpread false`) stops fire from spreading and burning blocks away; fires then only burn where they are until they go out. The showcase world has it off. A server can also switch spreading off for all its worlds with the limit `fireSpreadRadius` 0 in server.json.
chapter.qtcraft.fire.bodies.title: Burning players and creatures
chapter.qtcraft.fire.bodies.text: Whoever walks into fire or lava catches fire and keeps burning for a while after stepping out (fire 8 seconds, lava 15; see the block pages). While burning, a player or creature loses {fire.burnDamage} health every {fire.burnInterval} second; armour takes part of it like any blow. Water puts the flames out at once, and so does rain falling on you. Players in creative mode do not burn. Items that fall into fire or lava burn up.
chapter.qtcraft.weather.kinds.title: Clear, rain and thunderstorms
chapter.qtcraft.weather.kinds.text: The weather is the same in the whole world. A clear spell lasts {weather.clearMinutesMin} to {weather.clearMinutesMax} minutes; then it rains for {weather.rainMinutesMin} to {weather.rainMinutesMax} minutes, or, with a chance of {weather.thunderChance} in 100, a thunderstorm rages for {weather.thunderMinutesMin} to {weather.thunderMinutesMax} minutes; after that it clears up again. Rain and thunder come and go over {weather.fadeSeconds} seconds: clouds cover the sky, it grows darker, the fog comes closer and the sky lights the land less. Each world has its own course of weather, given by its seed.
chapter.qtcraft.weather.where.title: Rain and snow
chapter.qtcraft.weather.where.text: Rain and snow fall only where the sky is open: not under a roof, a tree or an overhang. In cold biomes (taiga, tundra) it snows instead of raining, and in every other biome it snows from {weather.snowHeight} blocks up (in the mountains from their snow line). In the desert it stays dry, although the sky darkens there too. You hear the rain around you, muffled under a roof.
chapter.qtcraft.weather.thunder.title: Thunderstorms
chapter.qtcraft.weather.thunder.text: In a thunderstorm lightning strikes now and then within {weather.strikeReach} blocks of a player, on average every {weather.strikeSeconds} seconds per player, only where it rains (not into snow or the desert). The flash lights up the sky at once; the thunder follows as late as sound needs for the distance: about three seconds per kilometre. A strike hurts everyone within {weather.strikeRadius} blocks by {weather.strikeDamage} health (armour takes part of it) and sets them alight; it may light a few fires where it strikes, but only while fire spreads (`fireSpread`) and within the limits of fire.
chapter.qtcraft.weather.effects.title: What rain and snow do
chapter.qtcraft.weather.effects.text: Rain puts out the fires it falls on, sooner or later (the older the fire, the sooner), and fire does not spread into the rain; fire on a magma block burns on. It also puts out burning players and creatures, and it keeps farmland under the open sky wet like water nearby. It never fills the world with water. Where it snows, a thin snow cover settles bit by bit on the tops of solid blocks under the open sky, not under a roof, on ice, glass or leaves, and only one layer per spot. Snow does not melt again.
chapter.qtcraft.weather.changing.title: Changing the weather
chapter.qtcraft.weather.changing.text: `/weather` shows the weather. Operators set it with `/weather clear`, `/weather rain` or `/weather thunder`, for a number of seconds (`/weather rain 120`) or as long as the course of the world says. With the game rule **weatherCycle** off (`/gamerule weatherCycle false`) the weather stays as it is until it is set again; the showcase world starts that way, with a clear sky.
block.qtcraft.lapis_ore.description: Deep blue flecks in the stone, rarely above height 30. Needs a pickaxe of level {qtcraft:lapis_ore.toolLevel} or better and gives several pieces of lapis lazuli and some experience.
block.qtcraft.lapis_block.description: Nine pieces of lapis lazuli packed into a block; crafting it back gives all nine.
item.qtcraft.lapis_lazuli.description: A blue stone from deep ores. It makes blue dye; traders and enchanting will want it.
chapter.qtcraft.experience.orbs.title: Experience orbs
chapter.qtcraft.experience.orbs.text: Mining ores (coal, diamond, lapis lazuli, Signal Dust ore), killing creatures, smelting in a furnace and breeding animals give experience as small glowing orbs. Orbs fly to the nearest player within {experience.attractRange} blocks and are collected with a chime; a furnace keeps the experience of what it smelted until a player takes the result. Orbs close together merge into one, and they vanish after {experience.despawnSeconds} s while their area is loaded. A world holds at most {experience.orbLimit} orbs; beyond that new experience joins the nearest orb, so nothing is lost.
chapter.qtcraft.experience.levels.title: Levels
chapter.qtcraft.experience.levels.text: Experience fills the green bar above the hotbar; when it is full you reach the next level, shown by the number in the middle, with a fanfare. Each level costs more than the one before: 7 points for the first, 17 for level 5, 37 for level 15 and 112 for level 30. Levels are what traders and enchanting will ask for.
chapter.qtcraft.experience.death.title: Experience and death
chapter.qtcraft.experience.death.text: When you die you drop {experience.deathPerLevel} points per level as orbs, at most {experience.deathMax} points; the rest is lost and you start again at level 0. With the game rule keepInventory you keep your experience, and so do players in creative mode.
chapter.qtcraft.experience.commands.text: Operators change experience with /xp add <player> <amount> [points|levels] (a negative amount takes away), /xp set <player> <amount> [points|levels] and /xp query <player>.
block.qtcraft.bed.description: Two blocks long: placed from the foot, the head lies one block further in the direction you look; breaking either half takes the bed. Villages count every bed head inside them; later villagers sleep in them.
block.qtcraft.bell.description: Hangs over the meeting point in the middle of every village.
block.qtcraft.composter.description: A wooden bin at the fields of villages. It is the farmers' workstation.
chapter.qtcraft.villages.finding.title: Finding villages
chapter.qtcraft.villages.finding.text: Villages stand on flat land in plains, deserts, taiga and tundra, and on stilts in the wet parts of swamps; never in oceans, mountains or forests. The world is divided into square regions (384 blocks in the base game), and a region holds at most one village, about half a region away from the next. Where a village goes depends only on the seed, so a world of the same seed has its villages in the same places. Operators find the nearest one with `/locate village`; `/village` shows its state.
chapter.qtcraft.villages.styles.title: Styles
chapter.qtcraft.villages.styles.text: Each biome builds in its own style. Plains villages are made of oak and cobblestone with pitched roofs of stairs, a well with a bell in the middle, main roads of cobblestone or gravel, side roads of dirt path and lamp posts. Desert villages are made of sandstone and terracotta with flat roofs, main roads of terracotta or packed mud that stand out against the sand, side roads of cut sandstone and fields with sugar cane by the water. Taiga villages are the plains houses in spruce. Snowy villages in the tundra mix igloos of snow blocks with ice windows, spruce cabins under a layer of snow and the larger plains houses in spruce, with main roads of packed ice or gravel. Swamp villages stand in the water on stilts of dark spruce: huts with thatched roofs, a meeting hall with the bell on a large platform in the middle, a fisher's hut, a herb hut with mushrooms and raised fields, all joined by boardwalks at one height above the water, with stairs down where a boardwalk reaches dry land. Around them the swamp is shallow water over mud. A biome that has villages but no style of its own (one a mod adds) builds in the plains style.
chapter.qtcraft.villages.buildings.title: Buildings
chapter.qtcraft.villages.buildings.text: Every village has its own street plan: one long main street through the middle with side streets, four roads from the well to all sides, three in a T or two in an L, a ring road around a square with the well, or roads at all angles that bend; some roads wind along the slopes. Diagonal roads run as staircases, and the houses at them have a forecourt to the road. Roads stop at water and steep slopes. Along them stand small and large houses with beds, fields of wheat, carrots and potatoes, ripe and still growing, with water and paths between the rows, a smithy with furnaces and a church or temple, each with its door to the road. Every kind of house comes in several designs, and no two houses need to look alike: walls of oak, birch or spruce, roofs of wood, cobblestone or brick, a chimney, flowers in front, a shed beside, terracotta in different colours in the desert. Some villages have an animal pen with a pair of pigs or sheep; a village near water has a fisher's hut with a jetty out over the water; large villages have a stone watchtower, taller than every house, with a ladder up to its battlements. Where a main road climbs a terrace by one block, a slab makes the step. Lanterns light the houses inside and lamp posts the roads, so no monsters spawn in them. Houses rest on a foundation where the ground is uneven, and the ground above them is cleared.
chapter.qtcraft.villages.state.title: Beds and workstations
chapter.qtcraft.villages.state.text: The world remembers every village: its middle, its area, its beds and its workstations (composter: farmer, furnace: smith, barrel: fisher). Beds and workstations you place or break inside a village count at once; one placed up to {village.joinDistance} blocks from a village's buildings joins it, and the area grows, but never into another village's: every bed and workstation belongs to one village. A bed or workstation farther from every village starts a settlement of its own: villagers without a home move in, and it lives like any village (children, golems). A settlement without beds, workstations and villagers is forgotten. Villagers claim a bed and a workstation each (see Villagers). A village lists at most {village.beds} beds and {village.workstations} workstations (one placed beyond that is not listed later either); the server limits `villageBeds`, `villageWorkstations` and `villages` change that.
chapter.qtcraft.villages.mods.title: Villages in mods
chapter.qtcraft.villages.mods.text: A style is a file in `villages/`: the biomes it builds in, the well, the lamp post, the kinds of buildings with weights and maximum counts, each with one or several designs, the street plans (main street, cross, T, L, ring road, branching roads, winding or straight), the road surfaces for main roads and side roads (one chosen per village, with an optional slab for steps), the crops of the fields and the foundation block and a palette that swaps blocks of the houses. A kind can have rules: a chance per village, a smallest village size (the length of all its roads) or water within reach (then it gets a jetty). A style can stand over water on stilts, with boardwalks for roads and the swamp around it shaped into shallow water over mud. The houses are ordinary structures; `choices` (block swaps, one option per house) and optional `parts` with a chance (chimney, flowers, shed) make every house different. A file with `extends` changes a style or makes a new one from it, and its `add` appends biomes, crops, kinds of buildings and street plans, so several mods can each add a crop to the plains. A mod can add a style for its own biome, a new style from the base game's houses with another palette, or new house designs.
mob.qtcraft.villager.description: Lives in a village with a bed of its own and, with luck, a workstation that gives it its profession. It works by day, meets the others at the bell, goes home in the evening and sleeps in its bed at night. It opens wooden doors and shuts them behind it, runs home from monsters and never fights.
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.homes.title: Homes
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.homes.text: When the part of a village with a bed is seen for the first time, a villager moves into every free bed, up to {villagers.perVillage} in one village. Each one claims its bed and keeps it; break the bed and the villager looks for another free one. A villager without a bed, or carried more than {villagers.strayDistance} blocks beyond its village's buildings (in a minecart, pushed or led away), moves into the village with the free bed nearest to it within {villagers.searchRadius} blocks. Villagers stay in the world for good: they wait while their part of the world is not loaded and are saved with it. Their clothes follow the style of their village: tunics on the plains, robes and headwraps in the desert, fur in the taiga, pale furs and fur hats in the snow, smocks and waders with reed hats in the swamp, each villager with its own colours.
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.professions.te: A villager without work claims a free workstation and takes its profession: the composter makes a farmer (apron and straw hat), the furnace a smith (leather apron) and the barrel a fisher (oilskin vest and hat). Each workstation belongs to one villager. Farmers harvest the ripe crops of every field within {villagers.cropRadius} blocks of their composter, yours too, and plant them again at once; the harvest stays with the village (no items drop). With the game rule `mobGriefing` off they leave the crops alone. A villager that loses its workstation before it ever traded is out of work again. Villagers with a profession trade with you (see the chapter on trading).
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.routine.title: A villager's day
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.routine.text: After sunrise villagers stroll about, then go to work. Around noon they meet at the bell and go back to work in the afternoon. Towards evening they stroll once more, at sunset they go home, and at night they lie in their beds until morning. A villager in bed gets up when it is hurt. When it rains in the village, everyone goes home. Monsters within {villagers.fleeDistance} blocks send villagers running home; one that is hit runs away too. They can be hurt like animals and do not fight back.
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.ways.title: Doors and long ways
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.ways.text: Villagers open wooden doors on their way and close them behind them; iron doors stay shut for them. A long way through the village, say across the boardwalks of a swamp village, goes along the roads in stages, so villagers find their way home from every corner of their village.
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.children.title: Children
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.children.text: A village grows into its free beds. Two grown-up villagers that meet by day, in dry weather, and each have food (at least {villagers.breedingFood} crops) get a child when their village has a free bed: the child moves into the free bed nearest to them. Farmers bring in the food: what they harvest stays with them, and a farmer with more than {villagers.shareAbove} crops shares with the villagers near it that have too little. The parents then rest for {villagers.breedingRestMinutes} minutes. A child is half as tall, has no profession, plays about the village instead of working and does not trade; after {villagers.growUpMinutes} minutes it is grown up and takes a free workstation. No child is born at night, in rain, without a free bed or beyond {villagers.perVillage} villagers in one village and {villagers.max} in the world. Throw them bread (worth 3 crops), carrots, potatoes or wheat and grown-up villagers pick it up as food until they hold {villagers.wantsFood} crops (not with the game rule `mobGriefing` off). So placing beds in a village makes it grow, and a bed left by a villager who died is filled again.
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.golems.title: Iron golems
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.golems.text: Villagers call an iron golem when they are in danger or gossip, but only those that slept in their bed within the last {golems.sleptMinutes} minutes. A villager panics when a monster comes within {villagers.fleeDistance} blocks, even in its bed, which wakes it. When a panicking villager has at least {golems.minVillagers} villagers that slept lately within {golems.gatherDistance} blocks of it (itself included) and no iron golem is within {golems.golemDistance} blocks, a golem appears somewhere within {golems.spawnRadius} blocks of it, on solid ground where it fits; glass, panes, leaves and ice carry no golem. Without panic, {golems.gossipVillagers} such villagers together gossip a golem up the same way, with a chance of {golems.gossipPercent} % every {golems.checkSeconds} seconds. A village summons at most one golem every {golems.cooldownSeconds} seconds, and villagers summon none beyond {golems.max} golems in the world. This works with a handful of villagers, so a small pen with three beds and a monster kept behind glass is a golem farm. Villagers summon golems even when creatures do not spawn by themselves. A village golem strolls within its village and walks back when it strays.
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.golem_building: Build an iron golem yourself: stand four iron blocks upright in a T (two on top of each other, one on each side of the upper one) and put a carved pumpkin on top, facing any way; the blocks beside the head and the foot must be empty. The blocks turn into the golem. Carve a pumpkin by using shears on it; four pumpkin seeds fall out. Iron golems guard villagers: they hunt monsters they see and throw them into the air with their blows. They leave players alone, but a player who hurts a villager or a golem of a village is its enemy for {golems.grudgeMinutes} minutes, and a golem that is hurt is angry with the player for {golems.angerSeconds} seconds; golems you built never attack players. Repair a hurt golem by using an iron ingot on it. A golem drops iron ingots and sometimes poppies.
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.mods.title: Villagers in mods
chapter.qtcraft.villagers.mods.text: A creature kind lives in villages with `"villager": "<settings>"`, naming its species' file in `villagers/`: the daily routine as steps through the day (wander, work, meet, home, sleep), how far it flees, trading, `breeding` (the food a parent needs, how farmers share, how long children take to grow up and parents rest) and the default look. Each profession is its own file in `professions/`: the blocks it works at, layers laid over the outfit, a hat, whether it tends crops, and optionally its own routine; two mods each adding a profession keep both. A village style dresses its villagers with `look` in its file (an outfit, hair styles and hats to choose from and lists of skin, hair, shirt and trouser colours), may name its own villager kind and golems and lists other residents. `worldgen/villages.json` names the villagers and the golem of all other villages and its thresholds.
chapter.qtcraft.trading.screen.title: The trading screen
chapter.qtcraft.trading.screen.text: Use a villager with a profession to open its trading screen. On the left it lists its offers: what you pay, what you get and how often it can still sell before it restocks. Pick an offer and its costs and result show in large slots; a click on the result trades once, a shift-click as often as your inventory pays (at most {trading.maxRepeats} times). The price comes out of your inventory; what does not fit into it falls at your feet. While the screen is open the villager stands and faces you, and only you can trade with it. The screen closes when you walk away, when a monster comes near or someone hits the villager (it runs home), and at night villagers in bed do not trade. Villagers without a profession only look at you.
chapter.qtcraft.trading.levels.title: Levels and experience
chapter.qtcraft.trading.levels.text: Every trade gives the villager experience; the green bar under its name shows the way to its next level. A novice becomes an apprentice at {trading.apprentice} experience, a journeyman at {trading.journeyman}, an expert at {trading.expert} and a master at {trading.master}. With each level it adds {trading.offersPerLevel} offers of that level, chosen once and kept for good, so two villagers of one profession can offer different things. You get experience too: every trade drops a few experience orbs, more for the offers of higher levels.
chapter.qtcraft.trading.restock.title: Restocking and prices
chapter.qtcraft.trading.restock.text: An offer can be traded a limited number of times. During work time a villager at its workstation restocks all its offers, up to {trading.restocksPerDay} times a day. An offer that sold out before a restock is in demand: the first thing it asks for costs a little more the next time, at most twice the usual price. Offers that are not sold out get cheaper again by one step at every restock.
chapter.qtcraft.trading.farmer.title: The farmer
chapter.qtcraft.trading.farmer.text: Buys wheat, potatoes and carrots (novice), pumpkins (apprentice) and melons (journeyman) for an emerald. Sells bread, apples, pumpkin pie, baked potatoes, sugar, hay bales and melon seeds, and as a master mushroom stew and a diamond hoe.
chapter.qtcraft.trading.smith.title: The smith
chapter.qtcraft.trading.smith.text: Buys coal and iron ingots (novice), gold ingots (apprentice), lapis lazuli (journeyman) and diamonds (expert). Sells iron nuggets, iron pickaxes and axes, an iron helmet and chestplate, a diamond sword, and as a master a diamond pickaxe and single diamonds.
chapter.qtcraft.trading.fisher.title: The fisher
chapter.qtcraft.trading.fisher.text: Buys string and coal (novice), sugar cane (apprentice), slimeballs (journeyman) and leather (expert). Fills your bucket with water for an emerald, sells lanterns, cooked mutton and fireflies in a bottle, and as a master slime blocks and diamond boots.
chapter.qtcraft.trading.emeralds.title: Emeralds
chapter.qtcraft.trading.emeralds.text: Emeralds are the villagers' money. You earn them by selling goods, or mine them: emerald ore lies rarely and in very small veins deep in the stone and needs an iron pickaxe or better. Nine emeralds make a block of emerald and back.
chapter.qtcraft.trading.mods.title: Offers in mods
chapter.qtcraft.trading.mods.text: A file in `trades/` lists offers of one profession: for each the level from which it is offered, one or two costs and a result (item and count), how often it can be traded until the next restock (`maxUses`), the experience for the villager and for the player and the price rise for demand. A file of another name adds offers to the profession; one of the same name as an earlier pack's replaces it. The experience per level, the number of offers per level and the restocks per day are set under `trading` in the villagers' species file in `villagers/`; a profession may set its own number of offers.
block.qtcraft.emerald_ore.description: Green specks in deep stone, rare and in veins of one or two. Needs a pickaxe of level {qtcraft:emerald_ore.toolLevel} or better and gives an emerald and some experience.
block.qtcraft.emerald_block.description: Nine emeralds packed into a block; crafting it back gives all nine.
item.qtcraft.emerald.description: A green gem and the money of the villagers: they pay in emeralds for what they buy and ask for them for what they sell.
item.qtcraft.bow.description: Hold the use button to draw it, release to shoot an arrow from your inventory. The longer you draw (up to {bow.drawSeconds} s), the farther and harder the arrow flies. Every shot wears it a little; in creative mode it shoots without arrows.
item.qtcraft.fishing_rod.description: Press the use button to cast the bobber, press it again to reel it in. When a fish bites, the bobber dips and splashes: reel in at that moment to catch something. Every catch wears the rod a little.
item.qtcraft.fishing_bobber.description: The float of a fishing rod. It floats on water until you reel it in; you cannot craft it.
item.qtcraft.arrow.description: Shot from a bow. Its damage grows with its speed; armour takes part of it. Arrows stick in blocks, where you can pick them up again until they vanish after {projectiles.despawnSeconds} s.
item.qtcraft.feather.description: Light and soft. Chickens drop them. With flint and a stick it makes arrows.
chapter.qtcraft.archery.bow.title: Drawing and shooting
chapter.qtcraft.archery.bow.text: Hold the use button with a bow in your hand to draw it and let go to shoot. A full draw takes {bow.drawSeconds} s and sends the arrow off at {bow.speed} m/s; a short draw shoots weaker, and a very short one not at all. The bow uses the first arrow of your inventory and wears with every shot.
chapter.qtcraft.archery.arrows.title: Arrows in flight
chapter.qtcraft.archery.arrows.text: Arrows fall in an arc and slow down, much faster in water. A hit deals more damage the faster the arrow flies and pushes the target back; armour protects as against blows. Arrows stick in the block they hit and fall when it goes; walk over them to pick them up. They vanish after {projectiles.despawnSeconds} s. A world holds at most {projectiles.limit} arrows in flight or stuck, and at most {projectiles.perChunk} stuck in one chunk (the oldest go first).
item.qtcraft.snowball.description: Thrown with the use button, one at a time and at once. It does no harm but pushes back what it hits, and bursts on anything it meets. Breaking snow with a shovel gives snowballs; four make a snow block.
chapter.qtcraft.archery.throwing.title: Throwing
chapter.qtcraft.archery.throwing.text: Some items are thrown by hand: press the use button with a snowball in your hand and it flies off at once. You can throw again after a short moment. A bow shoots only arrows, never snowballs. Snowballs fly in an arc like arrows, deal no damage, push the target back and burst where they hit. An ender pearl is thrown the same way and teleports you to where it lands.
chapter.qtcraft.archery.fishing.title: Fishing
chapter.qtcraft.archery.fishing.text: Cast a fishing rod with the use button and its bobber flies off and floats on the water. After {fishing.minSeconds} to {fishing.maxSeconds} s a fish bites (a quarter sooner in the rain): the bobber dips and splashes, and for {fishing.biteSeconds} s you can reel in with the use button to catch it. Mostly you catch cod and salmon, now and then a stick, string, leather, a bone, a bowl or even a bow. Reel in too early or too late and you catch nothing. The bobber is gone when you select another slot or walk more than {fishing.maxDistance} m away, and it is never saved with the world.
mob.qtcraft.skeleton.description: Comes out at night and lives in caves. Keeps its distance, circles you and shoots arrows with its bow once it has drawn it; it backs away when you come close. Its arrows cannot be picked up. Burns in direct sunlight.
mob.qtcraft.iron_golem.description: A big, slow guardian of iron. Villagers summon it when they panic or gossip, or you build it from four iron blocks and a carved pumpkin. It hunts monsters and throws them upwards; it is not pushed back by blows. Use an iron ingot on it to repair it.
mob.qtcraft.sand_golem.description: A golem of sand that guards the cellar of a desert temple and attacks whoever climbs down to its chests; it does not follow far. It is found nowhere else and cannot be built. Where it touches a water source block it crumbles into four blocks of sand in the shape of its build, with carved sandstone as its head; its arms fall as sand and can fill a water hole. In a dark cellar with no player close by, a new one comes back after a while: a renewable source of sand.
block.qtcraft.carved_sandstone.descripti: Sandstone with a face: the head that a sand golem leaves behind when it crumbles in water.
block.qtcraft.carved_pumpkin.description: A pumpkin with a face, carved with shears. Put it on four iron blocks in a T to build an iron golem.
item.qtcraft.shears.description: Carves a pumpkin into a carved pumpkin; four pumpkin seeds fall out.
item.qtcraft.bone.description: Dropped by skeletons. Crafted into bone meal.
item.qtcraft.bone_meal.description: Use it on a crop to make it grow {boneMeal.stagesMin}–{boneMeal.stagesMax} stages at once, or on a sapling for a {boneMeal.saplingChance} % chance that it grows into a tree right away. Each use takes one.
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.daylight.title: Burning in daylight
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.daylight.text: Zombies and skeletons catch fire in direct sunlight and burn for {fire.sunlightSeconds} s after they leave it. Shade, a roof or leaves above their heads, water and rain protect them, and so do caves.
chapter.qtcraft.farming.bone_meal.title: Bone meal
chapter.qtcraft.farming.bone_meal.text: A bone from a skeleton makes three bone meal. Used on a crop that is not ripe yet, it grows {boneMeal.stagesMin}–{boneMeal.stagesMax} stages at once; on a sapling it has a {boneMeal.saplingChance} % chance to let the tree grow right away, if it has room. Each use takes one bone meal, except in creative mode.
item.qtcraft.spider_eye.description: Spiders sometimes drop one. Its picture marks poison next to the hearts.
mob.qtcraft.spider.description: Climbs straight up walls and down again and leaps at its prey. By day in the open it leaves you alone unless you hit it; at night and in caves it hunts you. Wide: it does not fit through narrow gaps. Poison does nothing to it.
mob.qtcraft.cave_spider.description: A small, blue spider of caves and mine shafts, where spawners bring it forth. It climbs walls like a spider, fits through gaps one block high and poisons you with its bite. Always hostile.
mob.qtcraft.chicken.description: A small bird of the meadows. It flutters down gently instead of falling and lays an egg every five to ten minutes. Seeds of any kind make it fall in love. Drops feathers and raw chicken.
item.qtcraft.egg.description: Laid by chickens. Thrown with the use button, it bursts where it lands; one egg in eight hatches a chick there, and now and then even four.
item.qtcraft.raw_chicken.description: Meat of a chicken; better cooked in a furnace.
item.qtcraft.cooked_chicken.description: Chicken cooked in a furnace; good food.
mob.qtcraft.silverfish.description: A small grey pest that lives inside stone. It comes out when you break an infested block, bites, and when you hurt it, it calls its kin out of the infested blocks around. Left alone, it slips back into a stone block next to it.
block.qtcraft.infested_stone.description: Looks just like stone, but a silverfish lives inside. It breaks quickly even by hand, drops nothing and lets the silverfish out. Found in veins in the mountains.
block.qtcraft.infested_cobblestone.descr: Looks just like cobblestone, but a silverfish lives inside. It breaks quickly, drops nothing and lets the silverfish out.
block.qtcraft.infested_stone_bricks.desc: Looks just like stone bricks, but a silverfish lives inside. It breaks quickly, drops nothing and lets the silverfish out.
chapter.qtcraft.health.effects.title: Status effects
chapter.qtcraft.health.effects.text: Some attacks leave an effect that lasts a while. Next to the hearts a box shows each effect with its picture, name and the time left. Poison, from the bite of a cave spider, takes one health point every 1.25 s (faster at higher levels) but never your last one, and turns the hearts green. Armour does not help against it. Effects end with time or when you die; zombies, skeletons and spiders are immune to poison.
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.spiders.title: Spiders and cave spiders
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.spiders.text: Spiders climb straight up walls and hang on to overhangs, so a wall alone does not keep them out; an overhang of one block at the top stops the wide spider, not the small cave spider. By day in the open a spider leaves you alone until you hit it; at night and in caves it hunts you and leaps at you. Cave spiders live deep in dark caves, always attack and poison you with their bite. They fit through gaps one block high.
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.silverfish.tex: In the mountains some stone is infested: it looks like stone but breaks much faster, even by hand, and drops nothing; a silverfish crawls out. Hit a silverfish and it calls its kin out of the infested blocks up to ten blocks around. Left alone, a silverfish slips into a stone, cobblestone or stone brick block next to it and waits there. Breaking blocks in creative mode lets nothing out.
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.chickens.title: Chickens and eggs
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.chickens.text: Chickens flutter down slowly instead of falling and lay an egg every five to ten minutes. Thrown eggs burst where they land; one in eight hatches a chick, and one hatching in 32 brings four. Chickens fall in love with seeds of any kind. They drop feathers for arrows and raw chicken, which you cook in a furnace.
mob.qtcraft.enderman.description: A tall, dark wanderer of the night. It leaves you alone until you look straight at its head or hurt it; then it chases you and hits hard. It teleports away when an arrow or a snowball hits it (they do not hurt it), and water and rain hurt it, so it keeps out of water and jumps away from it. Now and then it picks up a block such as grass, dirt or sand, carries it around in its hand and puts it down somewhere else; it drops it when it dies. Sometimes drops an ender pearl.
item.qtcraft.ender_pearl.description: Dropped by endermen. Thrown with the use button, it carries you to where it lands, on a block or a creature; the landing hurts a little, like a fall. You always arrive in a place with room for you, never inside blocks or water, and never on the other side of a wall or a roof; a pearl that comes down under water is lost, and so are your pearls still in the air when you die. You can throw the next one after a second.
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.endermen.title: Endermen
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.endermen.text: Endermen come out on dark nights, rarely and in every biome. Look at their heads and they get angry, and the farther away they are, the more exactly you have to look; look at their legs or past them and they stay calm. One you hit chases you, not whoever stands nearest. They teleport to a safe place nearby: when they stand in water or the rain, when a projectile hits them and sometimes to reach the player they chase. They only ever land on solid ground with room above and only where the world is loaded. With the game rule **mobGriefing** they pick up single blocks and put them down elsewhere; an enderman carrying a block stays in the world until it puts it down. Without the rule it changes no blocks and drops a block it carries as an item.
mob.qtcraft.wolf.description: A grey hunter of forests, taiga and tundra that roams in packs. It leaves you alone until you hit one; then the whole pack nearby chases you. Feed it bones: each bone tames it with a chance of one in three, and it becomes your dog.
mob.qtcraft.dog.description: A tamed wolf with a red collar. It belongs to you, also when you are offline: it follows you, teleports to you when you are far away (only to a safe place in loaded chunks) and fights what hurts you and what you hit, never you or your other pets. Use it to make it sit or stand up; meat heals it, a dye colours its collar.
mob.qtcraft.cat.description: A cat of the villages, a few in every village. Feed it raw cod: each fish tames it with a chance of one in three. A tame cat follows you, sits when you use it and teleports to you like a dog, but does not fight. Creatures that are scared of cats keep away from it.
mob.qtcraft.ocelot.description: A shy spotted cat of the jungle (until there is one, of swamps). It runs away from anyone who comes close, unless you hold raw cod and sneak up slowly. It cannot be tamed; two fed with raw cod get a young one.
item.qtcraft.raw_cod.description: A fish; tames cats and lets you get close to ocelots. Better cooked in a furnace.
item.qtcraft.cooked_cod.description: Cod cooked in a furnace; good food, and it heals a tame cat.
handbook.value.pet.defends: follows its owner, sits when its owner uses it, teleports to its owner from afar and fights what hurts its owner or what its owner hits
handbook.value.pet.follows: follows its owner, sits when its owner uses it and teleports to its owner from afar
handbook.value.collar: the colour of this dye at first; a dye used on it by its owner colours it
handbook.value.shy: runs from players closer than %1 m, unless they hold this and move slowly
handbook.value.pack: strike one and the others within %1 m chase you too
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.pets.title: Wolves, dogs and cats
chapter.qtcraft.creatures.pets.text: Wolves roam forests, taiga and tundra in packs: strike one, and every wolf of the pack nearby chases you. Feed a wolf bones to tame it; each bone works with a chance of one in three, and the tamed wolf becomes your dog with a red collar. Cats live in villages and are tamed the same way with raw cod. A pet belongs to you, not to your character on one login: it stays yours when you leave and waits, standing or sitting, until you come back. Use your pet with an empty hand or any other item to make it sit or stand up. A pet that does not sit follows you when you walk away and, when you are farther than 12 m, teleports next to you, but only onto safe ground in loaded chunks. A dog fights what hurts you and what you hit, never you and never your other pets. Meat heals a dog, fish a cat; a dye colours a dog's collar. Ocelots are shy and run from anyone who comes close, unless you hold raw cod and sneak up slowly.
block.qtcraft.spawner.description: A cage of dark iron with a small creature spinning inside. While a player is within 16 blocks it brings forth up to four creatures of its kind every 10 to 40 seconds, on dark cells of the 9 x 3 x 9 blocks around it, until six of them are near. Breaking it gives experience but no item; it cannot be crafted. Dungeons and mine shafts deep underground hold them.
block.qtcraft.mossy_cobblestone.descript: Cobblestone overgrown with moss. Dungeons and their corridors are built from it and from plain cobblestone.
mob.qtcraft.cow.description: A calm grazer of the meadows. Use an empty bucket on a grown cow to milk it; wheat makes it fall in love. Drops leather and raw beef.
item.qtcraft.milk_bucket.description: Fresh milk from a cow. Drinking it with the use button ends all status effects, poison too, and leaves the empty bucket.
item.qtcraft.raw_beef.description: Meat of a cow; cook it in a furnace for a filling steak.
item.qtcraft.cooked_beef.description: Cooked beef, one of the most filling foods.
mob.qtcraft.cod.description: A fish of any water, lakes, rivers and seas alike. It swims in schools, flops about on land and suffocates there after a while. Catch it alive with a water bucket.
mob.qtcraft.salmon.description: A fish of the cold waters of taiga, tundra and mountains. It swims in schools, flops about on land and suffocates there after a while. Catch it alive with a water bucket.
item.qtcraft.cod_bucket.description: A cod caught in a water bucket. Pouring it out places the water and lets the cod out; a released fish stays with the world.
item.qtcraft.salmon_bucket.description: A salmon caught in a water bucket. Pouring it out places the water and lets the salmon out; a released fish stays with the world.
item.qtcraft.raw_salmon.description: Meat of a salmon; better cooked in a furnace.
Use an empty bucket on a grown cow to milk it. Drinking the milk with the use button ends every status effect, poison too, and gives the bucket back. Cows fall in love with wheat and drop leather and beef. Cod live in lakes and seas, salmon in the cold waters of taiga, tundra and mountains. Fish swim in schools and only in water; on land they flop about and suffocate after 15 seconds. A water bucket used on a fish catches it alive; pouring the fish bucket out lets it go again, and a released fish stays with the world. Fish have their own spawn limit and take no room from the animals on land.
